items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Peter Warren leaves, and he was replaced by Rufus Reid.

ctx.x: Then this group, “Special Edition” goes through various evolutions as well because when David and Black Arthur Blythe leave then Chico Freeman and John Purcell come in. So, continually evolving but maintaining your vision for an ensemble sound, continuing to write for these groups. Do you want to talk about that evolution and what that leads to at this point?
Yeah… The change of personnel. Peter Warren leaves, and he was replaced by Rufus Reid. For a while we had Chico, Purcell and Murray I believe.
So you had a three (horn) frontline then?

items.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013
items.q: But Jack DeJohnette played more up on the beat, much more in front of the middle.

ctx.x: Well you just said something that makes me think about, is there such a thing as playing on top of the beat or behind the beat?

Oh absolutely. Absolutely. This is what I also work with the bass players. Because we have the pulse. This is a quarter note: one-two-three-four one-two-three-four. But that’s not the pulse. The pulse is [hand gesture] and a bigger pulse is [hand gesture]. So there’s a lot of things that can be done within the pulse. And the beat is actually this wide, and the center of the beat is here. Some people play over here, some people play it here, some people play it here. That’s what it’s like, and this zone over here.…
Here it is, right here. You fit in.
